title: Do Republican States Have a Better Quality of Life?
text:
While many of his fellow Republican governors were being washed out of office by the midterm blue wave, Florida’s Ron DeSantis spent Election Day reasserting the superiority of red-state governance. “My budget’s 117 billion,” he said at an event hosted by the Institute for Legal Reform. “New York State’s budget’s $268 billion. That’s more than twice the budget.” And yet, he argued, if you live in New York, “you’re not getting better roads or infrastructure. I can tell you that, because people that move here tell me how much better our roads are. You ain’t getting better services. They tell me it’s easier to get a driver’s license in Florida at the DMV than it is up there.” 

 The difference between New York’s and Florida’s spending doesn’t actually come down to roads; it comes down to the two biggest items in most state budgets: education and, especially, Medicaid. But the perennial debate about which state’s taxpayers get more for their money cannot be answered just by comparing budget lines. It depends on a philosophical question: What does more even mean? 

 Sometimes, budget lines are a pretty good place to start. On public schools, DeSantis has a point. Education spending accounts for as much as a quarter of the difference in the two budgets. New York spends about $32,000 per K–12 student, the highest of any state, whereas Florida schools spend roughly $13,000 per student, the sixth-lowest in the country. (Those numbers include federal and local funding, but the ratio is similar when looking just at the state-funded portion.) The difference is attributable mostly to teacher compensation. Teachers in New York are paid an average of $99,000, the second-highest rate in the country. Florida, meanwhile, pays teachers the least of any state: just $57,000 on average. (Only a small portion of this gap can be explained by New York’s higher cost of living.) The difference in benefits is even more stark: New York spends three and a half times as much on employee benefits per pupil as Florida does. 

 New York also pays those higher compensations to a much larger number of educators. It employs 56 percent more teachers per pupil than Florida and nearly 150 percent more instructional aides—a result of New York’s relatively small class sizes and relatively large portion of students in individualized education programs. 

 [ Marc Novicoff: A mediocre public-school education for just $40,000 a pupil ] 

 Does this extra spending help students learn? The answer appears to be: not really. According to the Urban Institute’s demographically adjusted National Assessment of Education Progress, Florida scores much better in fourth-grade reading and math, while New York scores slightly better in eighth-grade reading and math. Instead, the primary beneficiaries are the state’s teachers. And thanks to a state law known as the Triborough Amendment, when a public-sector union contract expires, it doesn’t really expire—the yearly raises for the members stay locked in. This leads mechanically to the teachers’ union only ever getting a better deal than it had before. 

 As big as the gap between the two states’ education budgets is, it’s dwarfed by the difference in Medicaid spending. According to estimates from the National Association of State Budget Officers, New York’s program for fiscal year 2025 added up to $89 billion, compared with $34 billion for Florida. Categorizing that money as state spending, however, is somewhat misleading. Medicaid is funded mostly by the federal government. The money flows through the states, which make their own decisions about whom and what to cover. In fiscal year 2025, New York received $52 billion to Florida’s $17 billion. 

 Florida hasn’t unlocked some secret efficiencies. It simply ensures that few people are eligible for Medicaid to begin with. President Lyndon B. Johnson envisioned Medicaid as a way to extend “the miracle of healing” to the poor, but in Florida, the poor aren’t covered unless they’re elderly, a child, or a parent living with their child. Even for working-age parents, the program covers them only if they make about a quarter of the poverty rate. This means that a single mother of two children becomes ineligible for Medicaid if she makes more than $7,200 a year. As a result, 22 percent of nonelderly Floridians in poverty are uninsured, as are 20 percent of those whose income is one to two times the poverty line. In New York, those proportions are 9 percent and 8 percent. 

 [ From the April 2026 issue: The impossible predicament of the uninsured ] 

 New York is generous with public health insurance, giving it to a large percentage of the population and then allowing the recipients to use it on a wide swath of services. New York chose to expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act. That decision allowed it to offer the program to everyone making up to 138 percent of the federal poverty line; 90 percent of the extra funding comes from the federal government. Florida, by contrast, is one of just 10 states that have refused to expand their program. 

 New York also uses public insurance to cover residents who make up to two times the poverty line through something called the “Essential Plan,” which is also funded through the federal government under the ACA. Florida has no such program and no Medicaid expansion, forcing many more people who can’t afford insurance without subsidies onto ACA exchanges; in total, these Floridians get $32 billion in federal assistance, none of which is counted in the state budget. 

 New York doesn’t just have more Medicaid enrollees; it also spends about twice as much on each of them. This difference comes down mostly to spending on at-home long-term care. The two states spend similar amounts per home-care user—about $55,000—but in New York, that group comprises 729,000 people, compared with just 82,000 in Florida. New York has defined eligibility more generously than Florida in this category for decades, but recent changes have ballooned the difference. New York’s Consumer Directed Personal Assistance Program, which allows Medicaid recipients to choose their own caregiver, including a friend or family member, has expanded from $1 billion a decade ago to $11 billion in 2024. The program was engineered to allow seniors who would otherwise end up in nursing homes to instead stay with family members. But the number of people in nursing homes hasn’t budged, suggesting that much of the extra money—at least half of which comes from the federal government—may be going to people for whom it was not intended. 

 Voters rightly demand that the government not spend money in wasteful ways. And DeSantis is correct that New York’s larger budget doesn’t translate one-for-one into better services. But he seems to assume that the legitimacy of government spending should be judged according to how it directly benefits the middle-class taxpayer as they go about their daily life—driving to work, waiting in line at the DMV, and so on—rather than how it benefits the intended recipients of that spending. In fact, voters in New York have decided, through their elected representatives, that they believe in the importance of compensating teachers and funding the welfare state. That’s less visible than a snowplow or a pothole repair, but it’s not less legitimate. Whether the residents of one state or another get more value for their money is not only about money. It’s about what they value.
